arXiv:0812.2923v1 [cond-mat.mtrl-sci] 15 Dec 2008

Impact ionization rates for Si, GaAs, InAs, ZnS, and GaN in the G​WGW approximation

Takao Kotani Affiliation: School of Materials, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, 85284    Mark van Schilfgaarde Affiliation: School of Materials, Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ, 85284
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We present first-principles calculations of the impact ionization rate (IIR) in the G​WGW approximation (G​WGWA) for semiconductors. The IIR is calculated from the quasiparticle (QP) width in the G​WGWA, since it can be identified as the decay rate of a QP into lower energy QP plus an independent electron-hole pair. The quasiparticle self-consistent G​WGW method was used to generate the noninteracting hamiltonian the G​WGWA requires as input. Small empirical corrections were added so as to reproduce experimental band gaps. Our results are in reasonable agreement with previous work, though we observe some discrepancy. In particular we find high IIR at low energy in the narrow gap semiconductor InAs.

71.15.Ap, 71.15.Fv 71.15.-m

I introduction

The electron-initiated impact ionization is a fundamental process in semiconductors where a high energy electron decays into an another low-energy electron together with an electron-hole pair [1]. The impact ionization rate (IIR), which originates from the coulomb interaction between electrons, is a critical factor affecting transport under high electric field, as described by the Boltzmann transport equation (BTE). It is important in narrow gap semiconductors, especially for ultrasmall devices. Impact ionization is also used in avalanche photodiodes, and to supply electron-hole pairs for electroluminescence. Recently it has stimulated interest as a mechanism to improve efficiency in photovoltaic devices[2].

The IIR has been calculated with empirical pseudopotentials (EPP) in order to include realistic energy bands [3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. Sano and Yoshii calculated the IIR for Si [4, 5] and obtained reasonable agreement with experimental data. They also studied other materials [6], treating the transition matrix element MM as a parameter (constant matrix approximation). Jung et al. [7] used an EPP to calculate the IIR in GaAs. They calculated MM including explicit calculation of the dielectric function ϵ⁡(𝐪,ω)\epsilon({\bf q},\omega), rather than assuming a model form.

Recently, two groups have calculated the IRR using the density-functional formalism to generate the one-body eigenfunctions and energy bands. Because the standard local density approximation (LDA) underestimates semiconductor bandgaps while the IIR is very sensitive to this quantity, the standard LDA is not suitable. Picozzi et al. used a screened-exchange generalization[8] of the LDA [9, 10], and Kuligk et al. employed the exact exchange[11, 12] formalism [13]. Both groups used model dielectric functions for the dynamically screened coulomb interaction W⁡(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)W({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime},\omega).

Here we will present (nearly) ab initio calculations of the IIR without model assumptions. First, our noninteracting hamiltonian H0H^{0} is generated within quasiparticle self-consistent G​WGW (QSGW) formalism. We have shown that QSGW works very well for wide range of materials [14, 15, 16, 17, 18]. Because the IIR is highly sensitive to the bandgap, we add a small empirical scaling of the exchange-correlation potential so as to reproduce the experimental fundamental gap EGE_{G}. Corrections for semiconductors are small and systematic as shown below. Second, WW is calculated from the QSGW noninteracting hamiltonian. The IIR is identified with the decay rate (or linewidth) of the quasiparticle (QP), which is calculated from the imaginary part of the self-energy, as we describe below. Our method thus contains only one parameter, to correct the band gap. As we have shown[19], this parameter is small and is approximately independent of material. In principle our method can predict the IIR in unknown systems, and also for inhomogeneous systems such as grain boundaries, quantum dots, or impurities, where the IIR should be strongly enhanced because momentum conservation is much more easily satisfied. Thus the present ab initio method should be superior to prior approaches. Applications to such systems will be useful in devices that need to suppress or enhance electron-hole pair-generation from impact ionization.

After a theoretical discussion, we present some results. They are in reasonable agreement with previous calculations, except for InAs where IIR is calculated to be much higher than what Sano and Yoshii found [6].

II Method

The first step is to determine a good one-body Hamiltonian H0H^{0} which describes QPs. We obtain H0H^{0} from QSGW calculations[14, 15, 16]. As we explain in Sec.III, we follow Ref.[19], and modify H0H^{0} by a simple empirical scaling (α\alpha-correction) to ensure the fundamental gap reproduces experiment. From this modified H0H^{0} we obtain a set of eigenvalues {ε𝐤​n}\{\varepsilon_{{{\bf k}}n}\} and eigenfunctions {Ψ𝐤​n}\{\Psi_{{\bf k}n}\}, which are used to calculate the self-energy Σ⁡(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)\Sigma({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime},\omega) within the G​WGWA, Σ=i​G×W\Sigma=iG\times W. The inverse of the QP lifetime τ𝐤​n−1\tau_{{\bf k}n}^{-1} is obtained from the imaginary part of Σ\Sigma as

τ𝐤​n−1=2​Z𝐤​nℏ​|Im​Σ𝐤​n|,\displaystyle\tau_{{\bf k}n}^{-1}=\frac{2Z_{{\bf k}n}}{\hbar}\left|{\rm Im}\Sigma_{{\bf k}n}\right|, (1)

where Im​Σ𝐤​n=⟨Ψ𝐤​n|Im​Σ​(ε𝐤​n)|Ψ𝐤​n⟩=∫d3​r​∫d3​r′​Ψ𝐤​n∗​(𝐫)​Im​Σ​(𝐫,𝐫′,ε𝐤​n)​Ψ𝐤​n​(𝐫′){\rm Im}\Sigma_{{\bf k}n}=\langle\Psi_{{\bf k}n}|{\rm Im}\Sigma({\varepsilon_{{\bf k}n}})|\Psi_{{\bf k}n}\rangle=\int d^{3}r\int d^{3}r^{\prime}\Psi_{{\bf k}n}^{*}({\bf r}){\rm Im}\Sigma({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime},{\varepsilon_{{\bf k}n}})\Psi_{{\bf k}n}({\bf r}^{\prime}). By Im​Σ​(ε𝐤​n){\rm Im}\Sigma({\varepsilon_{{\bf k}n}}) we mean the anti-hermitian part. Z𝐤​nZ_{{\bf k}n} is the wave function renormalization factor to represent the QP weight. 𝐤{{\bf k}} denotes the wave vector in the first Brillouin zone (BZ), and nn the band index. The expression Eq.1 for τ𝐤​n−1\tau_{{\bf k}n}^{-1} is derived in Appendix B of Ref.[20]. Im​Σ{\rm Im}\Sigma is obtained from the the imaginary part of the convolution of GG and WW. For an unoccupied state 𝐤​n{\bf k}n, it is

Im​Σ𝐤​n\displaystyle{\rm Im}\Sigma_{{\bf k}n} =\displaystyle= −∫d3rd3r′∑𝐤′​n′Ψ𝐤​n∗(𝐫)Ψ𝐤′​n′(𝐫)Ψ𝐤′​n′∗(𝐫′)Ψ𝐤​n(𝐫′)\displaystyle-\int d^{3}rd^{3}r^{\prime}\sum_{{\bf k}^{\prime}n^{\prime}}\Psi_{{\bf k}n}^{*}({\bf r})\Psi_{{\bf k}^{\prime}n^{\prime}}({\bf r})\Psi_{{\bf k}^{\prime}n^{\prime}}^{*}({\bf r}^{\prime})\Psi_{{\bf k}n}({\bf r}^{\prime}) (2)
×\displaystyle\times π​Im​W​(𝐫,𝐫′,ε𝐤​n−ε𝐤′​n′),\displaystyle\pi{\rm Im}W({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime},{\varepsilon_{{\bf k}n}}-\varepsilon_{{\bf k}^{\prime}n^{\prime}}),

where states 𝐤′​n′{\bf k}^{\prime}n^{\prime} are restricted to those for which εF<ε𝐤′​n′<ε𝐤​n\varepsilon_{\rm F}<\varepsilon_{{\bf k}^{\prime}n^{\prime}}<\varepsilon_{{\bf k}n}. WW is calculated in the random phase approximation (RPA) as

W=v+v​χ​v=(1−v​χ0)−1​v,\displaystyle W=v+v\chi v=(1-v\chi_{0})^{-1}v, (3)

where vv is the coulomb interaction; χ\chi is the full polarization function in the RPA, and χ0\chi_{0} is the non-interacting polarization function. With Eqs.(1,2,3), τ𝐤​n−1\tau_{{\bf k}n}^{-1} is calculated from H0H^{0} in principle. In the Lehmann representation, χ\chi is

χ⁡(𝐫,𝐫′,ω)=∑m⟨0|n^​(𝐫)|m⟩​⟨m​|n^​(𝐫′)|​0⟩\displaystyle\chi({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime},\omega)=\sum_{m}\langle 0|\hat{n}({\bf r})|m\rangle\langle m|\hat{n}({\bf r}^{\prime})|0\rangle
×(1ω−ωm−i​δ−1ω+ωm+i​δ),\displaystyle\times\left(\frac{1}{\omega-\omega_{m}-i\delta}-\frac{1}{\omega+\omega_{m}+i\delta}\right), (4)

where |m⟩|m\rangle denotes the eigenstates (intermediate states) with excitation energy ωm\omega_{m} relative to the ground state |0⟩|0\rangle. Here n^​(𝐫)\hat{n}({\bf r}) is the density operator.

In the RPA, |m⟩|m\rangle are the eigenfunctions of a two-body (one electron and one hole) eigenvalue problem in the RPA. In simple cases such as the homogeneous electron gas, |m⟩|m\rangle for high ωm\omega_{m} are identified as plasmons; |m⟩|m\rangle for low ωm\omega_{m} are as independent motions of an electron and a hole. Thus τ𝐤​n−1\tau_{{\bf k}n}^{-1} for low energy electrons calculated in G​WGWA can be identified as the transition probability to such states for the independent motion of an electron and a hole together with an electron; that is, we identify τ𝐤​n−1\tau_{{\bf k}n}^{-1} as the IIR.

There are some questionable points for the identification. It might be not so easy in some cases to identify a state |m⟩|m\rangle as such a independent motion because the electron-hole pair can be hybridized with plasmons. However, such hybridization is sufficiently small for the simple semiconductors treated here, because plasmons appear only at high energies as ωm≳\omega_{m}\gtrsim 1 Ry. Another problem is that the final state consisting of two electrons and one hole is not symmetrized for the electrons in the G​WGWA. Thus Fermi statistics are not satisfied. Below we discuss how much error it causes.

Our formula Eq. (1) for τ𝐤​n−1\tau_{{\bf k}n}^{-1} is different from the customary expression found in the literature [3, 4, 5, 6, 7], e.g, see Eq.(1) in Ref.[3]. It is written as

τ𝐤​n−1\displaystyle\tau_{{\bf k}n}^{-1} =\displaystyle= 4​πℏ​∑𝐤′​n′∑𝐤1​n1∑𝐤2​n2|M|2\displaystyle\frac{4\pi}{\hbar}\sum_{{\bf k}^{\prime}n^{\prime}}\sum_{{\bf k}_{1}n_{1}}\sum_{{\bf k}_{2}n_{2}}|M|^{2} (5)
×δ⁡(ε𝐤​n−ε𝐤′​n′−ε𝐤1​n1+ε𝐤2​n2),\displaystyle\times\delta({\varepsilon_{{\bf k}n}}-\varepsilon_{{\bf k}^{\prime}n^{\prime}}-\varepsilon_{{\bf k}_{1}n_{1}}+\varepsilon_{{\bf k}_{2}n_{2}}),

where |M|2=12​(|MD|2+|ME|2+|MD−ME|2)|M|^{2}=\frac{1}{2}(|M_{\rm D}|^{2}+|M_{\rm E}|^{2}+|M_{\rm D}-M_{\rm E}|^{2}) includes both direct and exchange processes. The sum over 𝐤′,𝐤1,𝐤2{\bf k}^{\prime},{\bf k}_{1},{\bf k}_{2} is restricted to satisfy 𝐤=𝐤′+𝐤1−𝐤2{\bf k}={\bf k}^{\prime}+{\bf k}_{1}-{\bf k}_{2}. The matrix element MDM_{\rm D} for the direct process is

MD\displaystyle M_{\rm D} =\displaystyle= |∫d3rd3r′′Ψ𝐤​n(𝐫)Ψ𝐤′​n′∗(𝐫)×\displaystyle\Bigg|\int d^{3}rd^{3}r^{\prime\prime}\Psi_{{\bf k}n}({\bf r})\Psi_{{\bf k}^{\prime}n^{\prime}}^{*}({\bf r})\times (6)
W(𝐫,𝐫′′,ε𝐤​n−ε𝐤′​n′)Ψ𝐤1​n1∗(𝐫′′)Ψ𝐤2​n2(𝐫′′)|.\displaystyle W({\bf r},{\bf r}^{\prime\prime},{\varepsilon_{{\bf k}n}}-\varepsilon_{{\bf k}^{\prime}n^{\prime}})\Psi_{{\bf k}_{1}n_{1}}^{*}({\bf r}^{\prime\prime})\Psi_{{\bf k}_{2}n_{2}}({\bf r}^{\prime\prime})\Bigg|.

MEM_{\rm E} for the exchange process is the same as MDM_{\rm D}, except that the two electrons in final states (𝐤′​n′↔𝐤1​n1{\bf k}^{\prime}n^{\prime}\leftrightarrow{\bf k}_{1}n_{1}) are exchanged. Eq. (5) can be derived in time-dependent perturbation theory, where the final states consists of two electrons and one hole. This is based on the physical picture that WW causes transitions between the Fock states made of QPs. However, the final states made of the three QPs are interacting each other. Thus such a picture do not necessarily well-defined. This is related to a fundamental problem about how to mimic the quantum theory by the BTE. Definition of the IIR suitable for the BTE is somehow ambiguous. The difference between Eq. (1) and Eq. (5) is related to the ambiguity. One is not necessarily better than the other.

To compare Eq. (1) with Eq. (5), let us assume that Imχ0\chi_{0} is small enough. Then we have

Im​W≈WR​Im​χ0​WR\displaystyle{\rm Im}W\approx W_{\rm R}\ {\rm Im}\chi_{0}\ W_{\rm R} (7)

from Eq. (3), where WR=(1−v​Re​χ0)−1​vW_{\rm R}=(1-v{\rm Re}\chi_{0})^{-1}v. Reχ0\chi_{0} denotes the hermitian (real) part of χ0\chi_{0}. If we apply Eq. (7) to Eq. (2), Eq. (1) is reduced to an expression similar to Eq. (5):

τ𝐤​n−1\displaystyle\tau_{{\bf k}n}^{-1} ≈\displaystyle\approx 4​π​Z𝐤​nℏ​∑𝐤′​n′∑𝐤1​n1∑𝐤2​n2|MD|2\displaystyle\frac{4\pi Z_{{\bf k}n}}{\hbar}\sum_{{\bf k}^{\prime}n^{\prime}}\sum_{{\bf k}_{1}n_{1}}\sum_{{\bf k}_{2}n_{2}}|M_{\rm D}|^{2} (8)
×δ⁡(ε𝐤​n−ε𝐤′​n′−ε𝐤1​n1+ε𝐤2​n2),\displaystyle\times\delta({\varepsilon_{{\bf k}n}}-\varepsilon_{{\bf k}^{\prime}n^{\prime}}-\varepsilon_{{\bf k}_{1}n_{1}}+\varepsilon_{{\bf k}_{2}n_{2}}),

where MDM_{\rm D} is defined in Eq. (6) but with WRW_{\rm R} instead of WW. Through Eq. (8) we can elucidate the differences between Eq. (1) and Eq. (5) as follows:

  • (a)

    Eq. (8) (and thus Eq. (1)) contain the ZZ factor. This is because Eq. (5) was derived without taking into account the modification of QPs by the coulomb interaction. Typically Z𝐤​nZ_{{\bf k}n} is ∼0.8\sim 0.8.

  • (b)

    Eq. (8) and Eq. (1) do not include MEM_{\rm E} contributions. In the extreme case when ME=12​MDM_{\rm E}=\frac{1}{2}M_{\rm D} , |M|2=0.75×|MD|2|M|^{2}=0.75\times|M_{\rm D}|^{2}. This occurs in the Hubbard model when WW is a point interaction; the Feynman diagrams for MDM_{\rm D} and MEM_{\rm E} become the same except for their sign. Theoretically, including MEM_{\rm E} is advantageous because it symmetrizes the two electrons in the final state (though only for Im​χ0{\rm Im}\chi_{0} in the linear response regime). Fermi statistics are not perfectly satisfied because not all the exchange-pair diagrams are included. Omitting the exchange contribution reduces the IIR by a factor 0.75 at most, as explained above.

  • (c)

    Eq. (8) contains only the real part of WW, in contrast to Eq. (5). The difference originates from higher order contributions to Im​χ0{\rm Im}\chi_{0}. Moreover, when Eq. (7) is not satisfied there are further higher-order contributions to Im​χ0{\rm Im}\chi_{0}.

We may have to pay attention to these differences. For small Im​χ0{\rm Im}\chi_{0}, (a) and (b) predominate, and the difference between Eq. (1) and the Kane formula Eq. (5) should be a factor in the range 0.50.5 to 1. However, this difference is relatively minor on the log scale in the Figure.

III results

Here we treat Si, GaAs, InAs, zincblende ZnS, and wurtzite GaN. For each material we calculate a self-consistent noninteracting hamiltonian H0H^{0} through the QSGW formalism. Spin-orbit coupling is neglected, following prior work [6, 7]. Table 1 shows calculated values at high-symmetry points, compared with available experimental data. As we and others have noted[16, 15, 22], the QSGW gap is systematically overestimated because the RPA underestimates the screening. (Also the GaAs calculation used a smaller basis what was reported in [15], resulting in an additional overestimate of ∼\sim0.05 eV.) To compare the QSGW results to experiment, we must take into account other contributions: spin-orbit coupling, zero-point motion[23], and finite temperature all reduce the gap slightly[24].

To obtain the most reliable IIR, we slightly modify H0H^{0} to reproduce the experimental gap at room temperature without including these contributions explicitly. To do this, we add an empirical scaling (“QSGWα\alpha” correction) following the procedure used in Ref.[19]. We scale the one-body Hamiltonian as follows:

Hα=H0+(1−α)​(Σ~−VxcLDA)\displaystyle H^{\alpha}=H^{0}+(1-\alpha)(\widetilde{\Sigma}-V_{\rm xc}^{\rm LDA}) (9)

where Σ~\widetilde{\Sigma} is the static version of the self-energy (see Eq.(10) in Ref.[16]). Table 1 shows numerical values both with and without the scaling. As we showed in Ref.[19], effective masses are also well reproduced. Thus we can set up a satisfactory HαH^{\alpha} with a single parameter α\alpha. This procedure is reasonable because the uncorrected gaps are already close to experiment and 1−α1-\alpha is not large. The materials-dependence of α\alpha shown in Table 1 originates largely from the dependence of SO coupling and finite temperature on material. If these were taken into account by improving H0H^{0} explicitly, a universal choice of α∼0.8\alpha\sim 0.8 would reproduce the experimental gaps in the Table to within ∼\sim0.1eV. (Alternatively, adopting the present procedure with a universal α∼0.75\alpha\sim 0.75 accomplishes much the same thing.) Table 1 shows that the experimental energy dispersions are also well reproduced where they are well known (Si and GaAs). This systematic tendency is found for many other materials, including ZnO, Cu2O, NiO and MnO [14, 16], and GdN[18]. It implies that the QSGWα\alpha procedure is broadly applicable with comparable accuracy to many environments, e.g, to InAs/GaAs grain boundaries. The QSGWα\alpha energy bands are shown in Fig.1.

Given HαH^{\alpha}, we perform a one-shot G​WGWA calculation using the method detailed in Ref.[16], and calculate τ𝐤​n−1\tau_{{\bf k}n}^{-1} from Eq. (1). To reduce the computational time we truncate the product basis for each atomic site to l≤1l\leq{}1. This limits the degrees of freedom for the local-field correction in the dielectric function. However, we checked that this little affects the results. To obtain Z𝐤​nZ_{{\bf k}n} in Eq. (1), we need to calculate the derivative of the self-energy ∂Re​Σ​(ω)∂ω\frac{\partial{\rm Re}\Sigma(\omega)}{\partial\omega} at ε𝐤​n\varepsilon_{{\bf k}n}, though ZZ contributes a relatively unimportant factor ∼0.8\sim 0.8. The main computational cost of the IIR calculation comes from the sum of the pole weights on the real axis; see Eq. (58) in Ref.[16]. This corresponds to the convolution of ImGG and ImWW, Eq. (2), after ImWW is obtained from integration by the tetrahedron method [16]. Fig.2 shows our results for τ𝐤​n−1\tau_{{\bf k}n}^{-1}. The xx-axis denotes the initial electron energy εin\varepsilon_{\rm in} measured from the bottom of the conduction band; εin>EG\varepsilon_{\rm in}>E_{G} is a hard threshold below which IIR is zero. The present results, depicted by large plus signs, are superposed on results taken from previous work.

The IIR has a typical feature as already shown in Fig.1 in Ref.[5], that is, the IIR as function of εin\varepsilon_{\rm in} are widely scattered at low εin\varepsilon_{\rm in} because of the limited number of transitions that conserve energy and momentum. The scatter diminishes at high energy because of an averaging effect which smears the anisotropy in the Brillouin zone as discussed in [5]. Our results for Si and GaAs correspond rather well to previous work. Details for the IIR are already well analyzed [4, 5, 6, 7, 13, 10, 9].

Turning to ZnS and GaN, we superpose our results on those presented by Kuligk et al. in Figs. 9 and 10 of Ref.[13], which include exact exchange (EXX) (solid symbols) and EPP results from Ref.[10] (open symbols). The EPP and the present calculations appear mostly similar apart from an approximately constant factor; however the EXX results show rather different behavior, particularly in GaN. This is likely because the EPP and QSGWα\alpha energy bands are quite similar to each other, but they are quite different from the EXX case (see Figs 2 and 3 in Ref.[13]).

A large discrepancy with EPP is seen only in InAs. Our data is superposed on the calculations by Sano and Yoshii [6]. We obtain high IIR at low initial electron energies εin≳\varepsilon_{\rm in}\gtrsim1 eV. Such high IIR comes from initial electrons near the conduction band minimum at the Γ\Gamma point. Since the band gap and effective mass are small in InAs, there are states not far from Γ\Gamma with energy εin>EG\varepsilon_{\rm in}>E_{G}, which can generate an electron-hole pair. This occurs only for InAs in the cases studied, but generally occurs for narrow gap semiconductors. For the discrepancy with results of Sano and Yoshii may be due to their constant matrix elements approximation, which is not suitable for such a narrow gap material (see Ref.[6] near Eq.(2)).

In conclusion, we have calculated the IIR for several materials in the G​WGWA, after a theoretical discussion of its application to the IIR. In principle, the method presented here will be applicable even to inhomogeneous systems such grain boundaries and quantum dots where we expect very strong IIR. The present calculations correspond reasonably well to prior work, with the exception of the narrow gap material InAs. High IIR would be expected universally in similar narrow gap materials such as GaSb, InSb, and InN. This indicates that careful consideration for the IIR might be required when we use such materials for devices.
